title: Oct 28 Python vs Rust main on /v1/messages
lede:
Overnight comparison of the all-Python proxy from Oct 28 against current main, where the router and native Anthropic /v1/messages both run in Rust. S3 and Prometheus logging are on in both. The two builds ran back to back in each of 21 rounds, on the same frozen traffic. Every request in all 168 measured runs succeeded and was counted in both S3 and Prometheus.

Rust cuts the latency the proxy adds by 40% at the median and 44% at p99, and the wait after the last token by 63%. It pays for that with 18% more CPU per request, 6 ms more before the first token, and 250 MB more memory across two workers. Every one of those differences went the same way in all 21 rounds, apart from p99 time to first token, where Rust was lower in one round.
meta: Python d06b889d41 (Oct 28 main)Rust main 91fc6c2071 (Nov 14, same build as the Nov 15 baseline)2026-11-16 01:47 to 09:36 UTC2 workers on 2 pinned cores, 4 vCPU host
findings:
What stands out

+13.5ms / req

Rust adds about 22 ms of work and removes about 10 ms of Python

Under load the Rust build spends 18.5 ms per request in Rust code and 3.3 ms converting values between Python and Rust. In return the event loop, parsing, Python logging and router selection get cheaper by about 10 ms between them. Stream reassembly for logging goes up by 1.7 ms. The net is the 13 ms of extra CPU per request in the table.

7.4ms / req

Encoding the S3 log payload in Rust costs more than the whole Python S3 upload did

render_on_loop in callbacks-python/src/payload.rs walks the Python logging payload and writes it as JSON, mostly in write_string and push_ascii escaping the 50k-token prompt. It runs as a callback on the event loop, so it holds the GIL while it works. The Oct 28 S3 logger did its JSON dump, signing and upload in 5.5 ms. Escaping with a bulk routine, or reusing bytes the request already has, is the biggest single saving on the Rust side.

+5.1ms p50

More work before the upstream call, so the first token is later

Time before the upstream call goes from 18.8 to 24.4 ms under load. The profile shows before_provider_request at 3.6 ms, decoding the call at 1.4 ms and pythonize plus json_from_py at 2.5 ms on this path, none of which exist in the Python build. Headers and the first token arrive about 5 to 6 ms later as a result.

−38ms p50

The stream ends much sooner after the last token

The wait between the last upstream token and the client seeing the stream close drops from 61 to 23 ms. This is where most of the added-latency win comes from. The Python build does more work between the last token and closing the response, while Rust closes the stream first and rebuilds the response for logging afterwards.

+34ms p50

One at a time, the post-stream work lands on the next request

With an instant mock and no gap between requests, Rust's first token is 34 ms later than Python's. The logging that Rust moved after the stream close still has to run, and the next request starts while it does. Under real traffic with gaps between requests this mostly disappears, as the load numbers show, but it is a fair picture of a worker that is busy all the time.

17ms / req

Rebuilding the streamed response for logging is expensive in both builds

build_complete_streaming_response costs 16.1 ms in Python and 16.9 ms in Rust, and pydantic __getattr__ misses cost 5.1 and 6.1 ms. This is shared Python code, so a fix there helps both and is the largest target left after the payload encoder.

These rows overlap where one function calls another, so they don't sum to the total.
method:
Method and caveats

Each round ran a load pair and a sequential pair with the build order shuffled, and every third round also ran a profiled pair, so both builds share the night's drift. Every run starts a fresh proxy, mock, S3 server and Prometheus directory. The proxy is pinned to cores 0 and 1, Locust to core 2 and the mock and S3 to core 3. Locust stayed under 9% of its core. Every Python response had no Rust header, and Rust served 86% of responses with the header, the rest being non-streaming responses that Rust serves without it.

Round 17's first load run overlapped with a draft of this analysis running on the same machine, so the whole round was set aside and run again after round 20. Profiled runs are never measured runs, the flame graphs give shares and the milliseconds come from the unprofiled load runs. The first profiled Rust run lost 47 streams when py-spy fell behind, the same thing that happened on the Nov 15 run, and is left out, leaving 7 Python and 6 Rust profiles. Some runs wrote one more S3 object than requests, a leftover from the run before, and no metric uses that count.

The Rust build is the same commit as the Nov 15 baseline, but its CPU per request came in at 85.4 ms tonight against 91.0 ms then. The container moved to another host between the two nights, so compare absolute numbers only within one night. Within this night both builds drifted about 3% slower from the first half to the second, and the paired change column cancels that.

Data

Per-run metrics and pooled summaries for each build: load_pool_A0.json, load_pool_N.json, seq_pool_A0.json and seq_pool_N.json. The paired per-round changes: deltas.json. The merged flame trees, subsystem tables and top functions: flame_A0.json and flame_N.json.
